claims.text: Cooling HfNbTaTiZr generates residual thermal stresses because different constituent phases or microstructural regions have mismatched thermal-expansion coefficients.
Residual thermal stresses control the creep behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual thermal stresses control the work-hardening behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual thermal stresses control the thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed comparison applies the same annealing treatment to HfNbTaTiZr followed by either rapid quenching or slow cooling.
Rapid quenching preserves a higher residual-stress state than slow cooling.
Slow cooling allows residual thermal stresses to relax and therefore provides the baseline condition.
The mechanical and dilatometric comparison is to be conducted between 600 °C and 1250 °C.
Residual thermal stresses alter dislocation mobility.
Residual thermal stresses alter interatomic distances.
Annealing or thermomechanical treatment can change hardness and tensile response in high- or medium-entropy alloys.
The cited treatment-dependent hardness and tensile results support residual thermal stress as the cause of those changes.
Quenched HfNbTaTiZr samples will have greater yield strength than slow-cooled samples.
Quenched and slow-cooled samples will exhibit different strain-hardening behavior.
Quenched and slow-cooled samples will exhibit distinguishable dilatometric behavior.
Quenched and slow-cooled samples will exhibit different elastic moduli.
Quenched and slow-cooled samples will exhibit different creep responses.
The residual-stress hypothesis is falsified if the two cooling conditions produce no statistically significant differences in stress–strain curves, elastic moduli, or thermal-expansion behavior.
